newsitem.title: UK: Emerging market investors heartened by Thai deal.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market investors heartened by Thai deal.

text.p: Emerging market investors, fearful of shockwaves from Thailand's financial crisis, breathed easier on Monday after international pledges of $16 billion to rescue the country.
Economists and fund managers in Europe said the deal was good for Thailand, the region and emerging markets in general.
"This could be the turning point," said James Hancocks, fund manager at Guinness Flight.
"It's certainly positive in terms of sentiment because it means the situation is now being addressed."

The loan lifeboat from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Asian nations, the largest since the $40 billion provided for Mexico in 1995, was expected to nip in the bud the fallout on other emerging economies.
Humaira Sheikh, an analyst at Australia and New Zealand Banking Group, said the decisive response by the IMF and the international community showed an acute awareness of the need to reassure markets.
"It's clear that the IMF and other countries have learnt from the Mexico experience that it is very important to give the right signals to the international investor community," she said.
"They have had a well-coordinated joint action which should give investors a nice warm feeling about the whole situation."
But markets would reserve final judgment until seeing full details of the IMF package which will commit the Thai government to implementing tough fiscal measures, she added.
"We still need to see how committed the government is to biting the bullet and taking long-term measures which are politically not particularly palatable."
Thailand's cabinet approved broad plans to cut government spending on Monday but will review details only on August 19.
Fears of contagion from Thailand -- long lauded as a model Asian "tiger economy" -- have tarred other emerging countries, primarily in Southeast Asia, but also as far afield as Poland and Brazil.
With the damage capped via the deal which will provide Thailand with $14 billion requested for 1997 and 1998, the unwarranted pressure on these markets should now ease, analysts said.

Asset markets in Indonesia and the Philippines, both hit by the Thai crisis, were seen as obvious winners. But Malaysia, which last week reported a sharply deteriorating trade balance, could remain vulnerable.
Neil Williams, economist at Sumitomo Bank in London, said much of the earlier concern about the global impact of the Thai crisis was misplaced.
"Where there are strains and cracks in Latin America and central Europe, they probably reflect regional peculiarities rather than global peculiarities," he said.
The bid to draw a line in the sand under the episode meant investors would again refocus on the attractive fundamentals and high yields of many less mature economies.
